Female Adriatic sole attain a significantly larger maximum body size than males, with field surveys reporting an ultimate total length of 29.1 centimeters [Li = 29.1 centimeters] for females, whereas males reach a comparatively smaller ultimate total length of 27.0 centimeters [Li = 27.0 centimeters]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is a common pattern among pleuronectiform flatfishes and likely reflects differential reproductive investment between the sexes. The onset of sexual maturation in both sexes occurs at a total length at puberty of 20 centimeters [Lp = 20 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to approximately two-thirds of the female asymptotic length. Individuals reaching this size begin to allocate resources toward gonadal development, with gametogenesis commencing shortly thereafter. The size advantage enjoyed by females presumably translates into greater fecundity, as larger body cavities can accommodate more developed oocytes during each spawning season.

Reproductive output in this species has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 18.8 °C [T = 18.8 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, females produce approximately 822 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 822 eggs per spawning event] with roughly one spawning event per day [F_R_i = roughly one spawning event per day] during peak periods, representing the maximum recorded reproductive rate for the species. This daily egg production rate is consistent with values reported for other medium-bodied soleids that exhibit batch spawning behavior over an extended breeding season. The sustained thermal regime of 18.8 °C appears to optimize both the frequency of spawning events and the number of oocytes released per event, although natural populations likely experience fluctuating temperatures that modulate this output throughout the reproductive window.

The early life stages of Pegusa impar are characterized by a remarkably small birth mass. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from pelagic eggs with an average wet weight at birth of 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], a value derived from an egg diameter of approximately 0.7 millimeters. This minute neonatal mass places the species among the smaller-born teleosts, reflecting the limited yolk reserves available to support the endotrophic phase. The lecithotrophic larvae rely entirely on their endogenous yolk supply during the first few days post-eclosion, before the onset of exogenous feeding and the critical transition to planktonic life. Survival during this period is heavily dependent on water temperature and the availability of suitable microplanktonic prey at first feeding.

Adult body mass exhibits a strong allometric relationship with length, with the maximum recorded wet weight reaching 507 grams [Wwi = 507 grams] in large females. This asymptotic body mass, estimated from the length-weight relationship for the species, represents the upper limit of somatic growth under favorable environmental conditions. At the onset of sexual maturation, individuals attain a wet weight at puberty of 161.5 grams [Wwp = 161.5 grams], which corresponds closely to the mass predicted by the species-specific length-weight equation at the pubertal length of 20 centimeters. The substantial difference between pubertal and ultimate body mass indicates that significant somatic growth continues after reproductive maturity, a pattern typical of indeterminate-growing fishes that allocate resources to both reproduction and further body size increase throughout much of their adult lives.

Longevity data for the Adriatic sole indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years] when maintained under stable thermal conditions at 18.8 °C [T = 18.8 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan, coupled with the species' iteroparous reproductive strategy, allows multiple spawning seasons over an individual's lifetime, thereby increasing total lifetime fecundity despite the modest daily egg production rate. Natural mortality in wild populations is likely influenced by predation pressure from larger demersal fishes and by the energetic demands of seasonal reproduction. The combination of a moderate growth rate, delayed maturation at a length of 20 centimeters, and a decadal lifespan positions Pegusa impar as a relatively slow-lived flatfish among its Mediterranean congeners, with life-history traits that reflect adaptation to stable benthic environments.
